content: Pityriasis amiantacea, also referred to as Tinea amiantacea, is a dermatological condition affecting the scalp. It is characterized by the presence of thick, shiny, asbestos-like scales that adhere tightly to the hair shafts and scalp. These scales encase and bind clusters of hair, often leading to hair loss. The condition can either be localized to specific areas of the scalp or extend across the entire scalp. Repeated removal of hairs embedded in the scales can result in temporary hair loss or, in some cases, scarring alopecia. This condition was first described by Alibert in 1832. It is considered rare and is more commonly observed in females. Pityriasis amiantacea can be challenging to diagnose due to its resemblance to other scalp disorders, such as psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, or lichen planus. However, a distinguishing feature of pityriasis amiantacea is that the scales are firmly attached to both the scalp and the hair shafts. The condition may coexist with other inflammatory skin disorders, including atopic dermatitis or seborrheic dermatitis, and can lead to sebaceous scaling and hair loss. According to the dermatology reference text Bolognia, pityriasis amiantacea is most frequently associated with psoriasis but may also occur in cases of secondarily infected atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, or tinea capitis. In most cases, the presence of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria is identified. Treatment with systemic antibiotics, in combination with coal tar shampoo, has been shown to effectively resolve the condition when bacterial involvement is confirmed. Additionally, fungal infections, such as tinea capitis, can mimic the symptoms of pityriasis amiantacea. In such cases, antifungal treatments are effective in resolving the condition. Physical examination of the scalp typically reveals the characteristic thick, adherent scales encasing tufts of hair. This clinical presentation is a hallmark of pityriasis amiantacea and is often documented in dermatological atlases for reference.
